title: Request for Extended Polishing Limits on Cabin Window Panes — Ionian Wings

ata.title: Passenger Compartment Windows — Cabin Window Assembly

abstract: Ionian Wings asked for the cabin window polishing allowance to be doubled so that crazed panes could be reworked in service rather than replaced, and the order was rejected on certification grounds with an alternative offered.

sections.request: We are replacing far more cabin window panes than we budgeted for, almost all of them for surface crazing on the outer face rather than for anything structural. Our shop can polish these out easily but the manual allowance runs out after one rework and then the pane has to go. We would like the allowance doubled, or a second rework permitted with an inspection, so we can keep panes in service. The current rule means we scrap panes that look and measure fine to us after polishing.
sections.background: We polish to the standard practice and we record every rework. Over two years we have replaced two hundred and eighteen panes across the fleet, of which our shop judged one hundred and forty could have been saved with a second polish. We understand the pane is a pressure part and we are not asking to change how it is inspected, only how much material may be taken off over its life.
sections.expected_outcome: A published second rework allowance with a defined thickness floor and an inspection to go with it, so that the decision to scrap a pane is ours to make against a written limit rather than a single-use rule.

type_data.business_justification: Two hundred and eighteen pane replacements in two years, of which the operator believes two thirds were avoidable, at a spares cost it estimates at 390 kEUR.
type_data.closure_note: Rejected. The polishing allowance is set by the residual thickness that the pane certification substantiation assumes after damage, not by a shop judgement of surface quality, and a second rework would take the outer face below the substantiated floor on the worst-case pane. No structural substantiation exists for a reduced floor and creating one would need a full pane requalification, which is out of proportion to the spares saving claimed. The operator has instead been offered the interim protective film introduced for a comparable crazing complaint on another fleet, and a review of the ramp cleaning agent, which the field service report suggests is the more likely driver of the crazing rate.
